Article Title: Oil prices extend losses as Hormuz reopening hopes ease supply fears
Article Text:
Brent crude fell 0.5% to $87.43 a barrel

Oil prices extended their decline on Thursday as hopes of renewed Middle East diplomacy raised expectations that the Strait of Hormuz could reopen, easing concerns over prolonged supply disruptions.Brent crude fell 0.5 per cent to $87.43 a barrel, heading for a fourth straight session of losses, while US West Texas Intermediate crude dropped 0.5 per cent to $81.86, on track for a fifth day of declines.The selling followed reports that Iran and Oman were working to finalise an agreement concerning the Strait of Hormuz, a critical energy route that handled oil and gas shipments equivalent to about one-fifth of global fuel consumption before the conflict began.Qatar's prime minister is also due to travel to Iran on Thursday to revive diplomatic talks aimed at ending the nearly six-month-old conflict. The US has halted attacks on Iran for about a month, while seeking greater economic pressure on Tehran.However, uncertainty over the waterway remains. Iran has indicated that Hormuz would not fully reopen unless the US meets its conditions under a ceasefire arrangement that later broke down.Analysts said the continued risk to shipping means a war premium could remain embedded in oil prices.Supply concerns are also emerging in diesel markets. US distillate inventories, which include diesel and heating oil, fell by 2.2 million barrels in the week to August 21, reaching their lowest seasonal level on record, according to the US Energy Information Administration.
Article Summary: Brent crude fell 0.5% to $87.43 a barrel, heading for a fourth straight session of losses. US West Texas Intermediate crude dropped 0. 5 per cent to $81.86. Selling followed reports that Iran and Oman were working to finalise an agreement concerning the Strait of Hormuz.

Article Title: Bank holiday today: Are banks open or closed on August 26 for Id-E-Milad? Check state-wise details
Article Text:
Bank operations will vary state to state on Wednesday

Can you still use banking services?

When will banks remain closed next?

If you are planning to visit a bank branch on Wednesday, August 26, you may need to reschedule your visit depending on where you live. Bank branches in several cities will remain closed today for Id-E-Milad, Milad-un-Nabi and Thiruvonam, while branches in other parts of the country will operate as usual.According to the Reserve Bank of India’s holiday calendar, banks will remain closed in Belapur, Bengaluru, Bhopal, Chennai, Dehradun, Hyderabad, Imphal, Jammu, Kanpur, Kochi, Lucknow, Mumbai, Nagpur, New Delhi, Patna, Raipur, Ranchi, Srinagar and Thiruvananthapuram.The closures are linked to Id-E-Milad/Baravafat/Milad-un-Nabi, with Thiruvonam also observed in Kerala. The holiday is therefore not applicable to bank branches across the country.A bank holiday affects physical branch operations but does not mean that all banking services stop. Customers can continue using ATMs, UPI, internet banking and mobile banking for most routine transactions, subject to scheduled maintenance.However, services requiring a physical branch visit, such as document submission, verification or certain account-related requests, will not be available at closed branches.Customers should check their specific branch's holiday calendar before visiting, as bank holidays can vary by city and state.Banks across India will remain closed on Sunday, August 30, as part of the regular Sunday holiday. The next major state-specific closures after August 26 are scheduled for August 28, when branches in several centres will close for Raksha Bandhan and other regional observances.
Article Summary: Banks will remain closed in Belapur, Bengaluru, Bhopal, Chennai, Dehradun, Hyderabad, Imphal, Jammu, Kanpur, Kochi, Lucknow, Mumbai, Nagpur, New Delhi, Patna, Raipur, Ranchi, Srinagar and Thiruvananthapuram. Article Title: 'A whole new vibe': Ashwini Vaishnaw shares glimpse of bullet train project taking shape
Article Text:
Ashwini Vaishnaw shares glimpse of bullet train project taking shape

India’s first bullet train is slowly moving from plans to pillars. Railway minister Ashwini Vaishnaw on Tuesday shared a glimpse of the work taking shape across Thane and Palghar, calling it, "a whole new vibe!" The 135.45-km elevated section stretches from Shilphata in Thane district to Zaroli village on the Maharashtra-Gujarat border.The route cuts through varied terrain, with 124.027 km of the section comprising viaducts and bridges, the National High Speed Rail Corporation Limited (NHSRCL) said in an official release on Tuesday.The construction is at different stages along the stretch. Pier work is underway across more than 100 km, while nearly 74 km of piers have been completed and are ready for viaduct girders.The work is being supported by nine casting yards, seven full-span launching gantries and eight SBS launching gantries, all currently operational in Maharashtra.Three elevated stations are also coming up along the stretch: Thane, Virar and Boisar. The Thane station has a concourse level around 12 metres above the natural ground level, a design aimed at protecting and preserving local mangroves in the eco-sensitive zone.The tunnels are making progress too. Of the seven planned mountain tunnels on the section, three have already achieved breakthrough, with drainage, waterproofing and lining work now underway.Bridges are another key part of the stretch, including a 460-metre bridge over the Ulhas River, a 2.32-km bridge over the Vaitarna River and a 510-metre bridge over the Jagani River.Overall, the section will have 36 bridges and crossings, including 12 steel bridges over major railway lines, the Mumbai-Nashik Highway and the Ulhas River.The release said the progress reflects the engineering work behind the project under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s vision and Railway minister Ashwini Vaishnaw’s drive to expand next-generation railway infrastructure.
Article Summary: Railway minister Ashwini Vaishnaw shared a glimpse of the work taking shape across Thane and Palghar. The 135.45-km elevated section stretches from Shilphata in Thane district to Zaroli village on the Maharashtra-Gujarat border. Three elevated stations are also coming up along the stretch: Thane, Virar and Boisar.

Article Title: Stock market operations on August 26: Are NSE, BSE open or closed today for Eid-e-Milad?
Article Text:
Stock markets have been quite volatile this week

So, is the stock market closed today?

What does a settlement holiday mean?

With Eid-e-Milad being observed on Wednesday, August 26, investors may be wondering whether they will get a trading holiday on the stock market. The festival is a holiday for several government offices and institutions, and banks in many states are also closed. But the stock market follows a separate holiday calendar.No. The NSE and BSE will remain open for regular equity trading on August 26, allowing investors to buy and sell shares during normal market hours.However, the day is a holiday for trade settlement.This means trading will continue as normal, but the clearing and settlement of funds and securities will not take place on the day.In simple terms, investors can buy and sell shares, but the actual transfer of securities or funds linked to eligible trades may be pushed to the next settlement day. Investors expecting shares or sale proceeds should therefore factor in the one-day settlement delay.The distinction is important because a trading holiday means the market is shut, while a settlement holiday allows trading to continue but pauses the settlement process.The currency market will remain closed on August 26, while commodity exchanges such as MCX and NCDEX will operate.The next full trading holiday for the Indian stock market is September 14 for Ganesh Chaturthi.
Article Summary: NSE and BSE will remain open for regular equity trading on August 26. However, the day is a holiday for trade settlement. This means trading will continue as normal, but the clearing and settlement of funds and securities will not take place on the day.

Article Title: TVS Motor appoints Peyman Kargar as CEO

Peyman Kargar will become TVS Motor's new Chief Executive Officer starting January 27, 2027

Article Title: India's hotel sector likely to gain momentum in H2FY27 on strong leisure demand
Article Text:
Resorts outperform city hotels as India's hospitality sector navigates travel disruptions (representative image)

Weddings, MICE activity and international travel to support demand

Corporate and international travel remained softer

Hotel companies report growth in Q1

India's hotel industry is expected to see stronger growth in the second half of FY27, supported by robust domestic leisure demand and a steady recovery in corporate and international travel, according to a PhillipCapital sector report.The hospitality sector remained resilient in the first quarter of FY27 despite geopolitical disruptions. Industry occupancy rose by 2-4 percentage points year-on-year, while average room rates (ARR) increased 6-8% and revenue per available room (RevPAR) grew 11-13%, the report said.PhillipCapital said the recovery could strengthen in the coming quarters, aided by a heavier wedding calendar, improving meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions (MICE) activity and a seasonal increase in international travel from October.Limited new hotel supply in key markets could also support room rates and RevPAR as demand improves, the report said.“Demand outlook remains positive for Q2FY27, with domestic leisure demand staying strong, corporate travel gradually normalising, and international demand recovering, as connectivity improves,” the report said.Demand in the first quarter was stronger in leisure destinations than in business-focused locations.For Indian Hotels, Rajasthan and Goa recorded high-20% growth in RevPAR. Chalet Hotels' resorts posted 19% RevPAR growth, compared with around 5% for its business hotels.Leela Hotels' resorts recorded 24% RevPAR growth, against 14% for its city hotels.Corporate travel remained softer during the quarter, partly due to geopolitical uncertainty and tighter travel budgets, while international traffic was affected by disruptions linked to the West Asia conflict.Domestic air passenger traffic grew just 1.2% year-on-year to 86.3 million in Q1FY27, while international traffic declined around 10.2% to 17.9 million. Total passenger movement fell around 0.9% to 104.2 million.However, PhillipCapital said the monthly trend improved as the quarter progressed.Domestic passenger growth rose 7.7% in May before normalising to a 1.2% decline in June. The decline in international traffic also narrowed from 18.3% in February to 4.7% in June, according to the report.Among the companies covered by PhillipCapital, Leela reported 28% revenue growth and 41% EBITDA growth in Q1FY27.Indian Hotels' revenue rose 15%, while its EBITDA increased 18%. ITC Hotels' RevPAR grew 8%, while Lemon Tree's occupancy improved by 314 basis points.“The Indian hotel industry delivered healthy growth in Q1FY27 despite geopolitical disruptions and normal seasonality,” the report said, adding that industry pricing remained intact even in markets where occupancy softened.
Article Summary: The hospitality sector remained resilient in the first quarter of FY27 despite geopolitical disruptions. Industry occupancy rose by 2-4 percentage points year- on-year. Average room rates increased 6-8% and revenue per available room (RevPAR) grew 11-13%.

Article Title: Nepal may need nearly a tenth of its economy to rebuild after devastating floods
Article Text:
A man navigates through a mud-covered street next to damaged houses following the flash floods and mudslide in Nepal

Over 600 killed, thousands still missing

Reconstruction estimate lower than 2015 earthquake cost

Nepal may need between $4 billion and $5 billion to rebuild after this week's devastating floods, finance minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters on Saturday, as authorities continued to assess the scale of loss and damage."The initial estimate is between $4-$5 billion. Just an estimate," Wagle said. "We will require much less than what we needed for the 2015 earthquake. Loss and damage is being assessed."The reconstruction bill would amount to nearly a tenth of Nepal's economy.A glacier collapse on Wednesday unleashed a huge torrent of rock, ice, mud and debris through Himalayan mountain river systems, killing more than 600 people in Nepal and China's Tibet. More than 2,000 people were still unaccounted for.The disaster levelled towns in the border region, sweeping away bridges and roads and damaging major hydropower stations.At least 626 people were killed in Nepal and seven in China's Tibet, while nearly 3,000 people remained missing across the affected areas.Nepal's disaster agency said 2,426 people were missing in the country.The floods also damaged power projects accounting for more than 12% of Nepal's national generating capacity, dealing a blow to an economy reliant on remittances, tourism and hydropower.Wagle did not elaborate on why the reconstruction cost from the latest disaster was expected to be lower than the approximately $9 billion spent after Nepal's devastating 2015 earthquake.The magnitude-7.8 earthquake, Nepal's worst recorded disaster, killed nearly 9,000 people, destroyed more than half a million homes and caused losses estimated at around a third of the country's economy.Meanwhile, search and rescue operations were temporarily disrupted by bad weather in some areas.Nepal has sought specialised foreign technical assistance, including help to rescue people trapped in tunnels, restore transport and communication links, identify bodies and conduct DNA testing.India has sent three flights carrying about 60 tonnes of relief material, including blankets, medicines, food and water purification tablets.
Article Summary: Reconstruction bill would amount to nearly a tenth of Nepal's economy. A glacier collapse on Wednesday unleashed a huge torrent of rock, ice, mud and debris through Himalayan mountain river systems. At least 626 people were killed in Nepal and seven in China's Tibet, while nearly 3,000 people remained missing.

Article Title: 'Such initiatives take time': Temasek supports Singapore Airlines backing Air India
Article Text:
Singapore Airlines owns 26% stake in Air India

NEW DELHI: "Efforts of this scale take time.." With these words, Singapore Airlines' (SIA) majority stakeholder and the city state's state investor Temasek has supported the airline backing Air India from a strategic long term viewpoint of having a second hub beyond Changi.The Maharaja has sought additional fund infusion of about $2 billion from Tata Sons (74.9% stakeholder) and SIA which owns the remaining 26.1% stake in AI. Singapore opposition MP Kenneth Tiong had opposed using state investor Temasek’s funds to meet AI request.Now Temasek has clarified its position in a letter to a business newspaper: "SIA has demonstrated discipline and resilience through industry cycles, and consistently positioned itself for long-term growth.... SIA has articulated its objective to invest in a second hub to secure long-term growth beyond Singapore. As the world’s third-largest air transport market after the US and China, India is well-positioned to serve as this second hub. ""SIA has long participated in the India market, including an operating presence through Vistara since 2013 and its investment in Air India allows it to deepen its participation in India’s aviation growth.As a shareholder of SIA, we view their business decision from a long-term perspective and are supportive of it. We recognise that the large-scale transformation of Air India involves complex, multi-year operational and integration challenges. ""Efforts of this scale take time and are not expected to be linear, particularly in the aviation sector, where outcomes are shaped by industry developments, including aircraft innovation and fleet renewal cycles, and external factors such as airspace disruptions, geopolitical developments and fuel price volatility. As we build a resilient and forward-looking portfolio, we support the strategic moves by our portfolio companies that position them for long-term growth and global competitiveness. While such initiatives take time, we believe that they are important for sustaining growth over the long run."SIA had Thursday said it will “carefully consider any requests for additional capital from AI, taking into consideration the group’s other capital requirements and AI’s business strategy.”AI has returned to its shareholders for funds more than a year after Tata Sons halted fresh equity injections into the airline, as its turnaround proves costlier and slower than initially envisaged. The amount would rank among the largest shareholder funding exercises since Tata Group regained control of the former state carrier in 2021.Tata Sons had paused additional equity support in the year to March 2026. Its investment in AI stood unchanged at Rs 22,618 crore in the FY2026 report, the same level as a year earlier — indicating no fresh equity was infused during the year.Air India reported a loss of Rs 22,238 crore in FY2026, more than double the previous year’s deficit and the largest among Tata Group companies. Air India has been the worst-hit Indian carrier from the closure of Pakistani airspace since last April, given the volume of flights it runs west from its Delhi hub — from the UAE to North America. The next blow came when its London-bound Dreamliner crashed in Ahmedabad last June, killing 260 people, forcing further flight cuts. The February 28 US-Iran war then sent oil prices higher and the rupee lower, lengthening Delhi’s already longer western routes and driving up operating costs — while Air India competed against western carriers overflying Pakistan on far shorter paths.
Article Summary: Singapore Airlines' (SIA) majority stakeholder and the city state's state investor Temasek has supported the airline backing Air India. The Maharaja has sought additional fund infusion of about $2 billion from Tata Sons (74.9% stakeholder) and SIA which owns the remaining 26.1% stake in AI.

Article Title: Russia has oil, so why is it importing petrol from India
Article Text:
Cars queue to refuel at a Lukoil fuel station amid fuel shortages following recent series of Ukrainian air attacks on oil refineries in Russian regions. (Reuters)

Ukraine hits Russia's oil refineries

Russia has oil, but it is short on petrol

Russia's fuel crisis in numbers

How Ukraine is hitting Russia’s oil lifeline

Russia has oil, but petrol is short

The shortage already visible before latest strikes

Russia is now importing petrol from India

India's petrol goes to Russia

India buys Russian crude, Russia buys Indian petrol

The pressure is spreading beyond petrol pumps

What does this mean for Russia’s war effort?

The bigger problem for Moscow

Russia, one of the world’s biggest oil producers, is now rationing petrol at home as Ukrainian drone strikes hit its oil refineries and disrupt fuel supplies.Reuters reported that petrol stations in Moscow have reintroduced limits on fuel sales as shortages return. Gazprom Neft has capped petrol purchases at 40 litres at automated stations and 60 litres at other stations, while Rosneft has limited sales to 30 litres per vehicle across Russia. Tatneft has also set a 50-litre limit.Long queues have also returned at petrol stations in Moscow and the surrounding region. The restrictions come after an earlier wave of shortages eased for a short period in July. But fresh Ukrainian attacks on refineries, along with strong seasonal demand and refinery maintenance, have again tightened supplies.The scale of the problem becomes clearer when Russia’s oil industry is taken into account. Russia produced about 9.89 million barrels of crude oil per day in 2025, making it the world’s second-largest crude oil producer after the US, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).The latest IEA data shows that Russia was still producing 8.76 million barrels of crude oil per day in July 2026.The figure was lower than the 8.86 million barrels per day recorded in June, but it shows that Russia continues to produce huge volumes of crude even as its petrol market faces shortages.Russia also has a massive refining industry. Its refineries processed about 5.4 million barrels of oil per day in 2024, according to the EIA. The country has major refineries spread across its vast territory, including facilities in Omsk, Kirishi, Ryazan, Nizhny Novgorod, Yaroslavl, Volgograd, Perm and Nizhny Novgorod.That is the key to understanding the current crisis. Russia is not running out of crude oil. It is facing pressure on the system that turns crude into petrol, diesel and other fuels.When a refinery is damaged or forced to stop processing, crude oil can still be produced, but less of it can be converted into usable fuel. That creates a shortage at petrol stations even when the country continues to pump millions of barrels of oil every day.Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities with long-range drone attacks. Kyiv has said the campaign is aimed at reducing Russia’s ability to finance and sustain its war effort.The latest attacks show how quickly the pressure is building. On August 26, Ukraine struck the NORSI refinery in Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region, forcing the plant to suspend crude processing, according to three industry sources cited by Reuters. The attack damaged several processing units, inter-unit infrastructure and other plant facilities.NORSI is not a small facility. Reuters described it as Russia’s fourth-largest oil refinery and second-largest gasoline producer. It can process about 15 million tonnes of crude a year and produce around 5 million tonnes of petrol, more than 5 million tonnes of diesel and about 2 million tonnes of fuel oil.The NORSI shutdown came just days after another major refinery was forced to stop. The Perm refinery, Russia’s seventh-largest oil-processing plant by volume, halted operations after a Ukrainian drone attack on August 21 caused a fire and damaged technological units.The attacks have also hit the Afipsky refinery in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region. The plant caught fire after a drone attack on August 25, according to the regional governor. Afipsky processed about 7.2 million tonnes of crude in 2024, equivalent to around 144,000 barrels per day.The repeated strikes are important because they are hitting the part of Russia’s energy system that produces the fuel used by its domestic economy. The damage does not have to destroy an entire refinery to create a wider problem. If major processing units are shut, overall output can fall even if other parts of a plant remain operational.The petrol crisis did not begin with the latest attacks. Russia had been facing supply pressure since the spring, with Ukrainian strikes on refineries becoming a growing problem.By early July, Russian petrol production had fallen to around 65 per cent of average seasonal demand, according to industry sources cited by Reuters. The estimated shortfall was around 40,000 to 45,000 tonnes a day, while summer petrol demand was around 115,000 to 120,000 tonnes a day.Russia began restricting fuel exports, using available stocks and increasing imports. It also relaxed some fuel-quality requirements so that refineries could produce more fuel for the domestic market. Reuters reported in June that the government was allowing some refineries to produce fuel with lower environmental specifications as Ukrainian attacks squeezed supplies.The first shortage wave showed some improvement in late July as some refineries returned to operation. But the recovery was short-lived. New attacks in late July and August again reduced refinery output, while strong summer demand continued to put pressure on supplies.The most unusual response has been Russia’s decision to import finished petrol.In July, Russia began buying petrol from overseas as domestic supplies tightened. Imports were coming from countries including Belarus and Kazakhstan, while Russia also turned to India for seaborne supplies.In August, the India connection became more concrete. A cargo of around 68,000 tonnes of petrol loaded at India’s Vadinar port reached Russia’s Arctic port of Vitino, according to LSEG shipping data and industry sources cited by Reuters. The fuel was then being moved by rail to domestic buyers.At least two more petrol cargoes from India were expected to arrive at Russian ports within two weeks of the August 17 report, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters. Industry sources had also previously told Reuters that the petrol was produced by Nayara Energy, the Indian refiner in which Russian oil major Rosneft has a stake.The India shipment is striking because the normal energy relationship runs in the opposite direction. India has become a major buyer of Russian crude.Russia remained India’s largest crude supplier during April-July 2026. In July alone, Russian crude accounted for a record 50.83 per cent of India’s crude imports, or around 2.47 million barrels per day, according to trade data cited by Reuters. Russia’s share for the first four months of the financial year was 43.25 per cent.India depends on imports for more than 90 per cent of its crude oil requirements, making Russian supplies an important part of the country’s oil market.That makes the current flow particularly unusual: India is buying huge quantities of crude from Russia, while Russia is importing some finished petrol from India.The two flows are not directly linked to each other, but together they highlight the difference between crude production and refining. Russia can remain a major crude producer while still needing to buy finished fuel if its domestic refining system cannot produce enough petrol.The impact is also showing up in Russia’s wider fuel trade.Russian seaborne oil-product exports fell sharply in July. Reuters calculations based on industry data showed exports fell 33.3 per cent from June and 54.7 per cent from a year earlier, to 3.93 million tonnes. Unplanned refinery maintenance linked to Ukrainian drone attacks was among the factors behind the decline.At the same time, Belarus increased its fuel supplies to Russia. Its gasoline exports to Russia reached 212,000 tonnes in July, up 13 per cent from June, while diesel exports doubled to 162,000 tonnes. From January to July, Belarusian gasoline shipments to Russia were 25 times higher than in the same period of 2025.This shows that Moscow is trying to fill the gap from several directions at once, by restricting exports, moving fuel between regions and bringing in supplies from neighbouring countries and Asia.Ukraine’s refinery campaign is not the same as destroying Russia’s oil production. Russia continues to produce large amounts of crude, and Moscow has several tools to manage a temporary refining disruption.But the attacks create a different kind of pressure.A refinery shutdown can reduce the supply of petrol and diesel available to civilians, businesses and transport operators. The government then has to decide where limited fuel should go, while trying to prevent prices from rising sharply and ensuring that essential sectors continue to receive supplies.Reuters reported in July that the Russian government was prioritising fuel for vehicles delivering food to large retail chains as the shortage spread. The central bank also warned that the drop in fuel production could hurt economic growth.The Kremlin can also protect strategically important consumers, including the military, from some of the effects of a civilian fuel shortage. Therefore, the current petrol crisis does not prove that Russia's military is running out of fuel. What it does show is that the energy system supporting the wider economy is under increasing strain.The most important question now is how quickly Russia can repair damaged refineries and restore lost processing capacity. Russia can compensate for some losses through imports and by moving fuel from one region to another. But if refinery outages continue, those measures become more expensive and harder to sustain.Russia still has the oil. It is still producing millions of barrels of crude every day. But Ukraine is increasingly targeting the infrastructure that turns that crude into the fuel Russia needs.For one of the world's biggest oil producers, the unusual part is no longer simply that petrol stations are imposing limits. It is that Russia is producing the crude while importing the petrol. And one of the countries helping to fill that gap is India, the same country that has become Russia's biggest crude-oil customer.
Article Summary: Petrol stations in Moscow have reintroduced limits on fuel sales as shortages return. Gazprom Neft has capped petrol purchases at 40 litres at automated stations and 60 litres at other stations. Rosneft has limited sales to 30 litres per vehicle across Russia. Russia is not running out of crude oil. It is facing pressure on the system that turns crude into petrol.

Article Title: Noel Tata, Shapoorji discuss share swap for Tata Sons stake sale
Article Text:
Tata Group in talks with Shapoorji Pallonji for potential share swap or buyout of its 18.4% stake in Tata Sons.

The Tata Group is in talks with its biggest minority shareholder on proposals to unlock liquidity, including a potential swap of shares of its listed entities, as the Shapoorji Pallonji Group seeks funds to repay costly debt, according to sources.Representatives of Noel Tata, the Tata family patriarch, are exploring the possibility where SP Group receives shares of companies such as Tata Power Co in exchange for some or all of its 18.4% in the privately-held Tata Sons Pvt, the sources said, asking not to be identified as the discussions are private.Two other options have also been presented: a direct buyout of the construction giant’s stake by Tata Sons, financed by overseas banks, or a sale to an external investor, preferably a global one, the sources added.Any breakthrough on this long-running tussle between the Tatas and the SP Group will prove to be a windfall for investors in the latter’s debt, which include the likes of Cerberus Capital Management LP, Davidson Kempner Capital Management and Farallon Capital Management. For the Tatas, a resolution may ease some of the intense regulatory spotlight it has come under in the past few years after RBI rules revived pressure on its holding company to list on the exchanges.Noel is the chairman of Tata Trusts, a group of charities that own 66% in Tata Sons. Natarajan Chandrasekaran’s announcement this month that he’ll step down as Tata Sons chairman in Feb has put Noel in the driver’s seat to drive a settlement. Noel also has familial connections: he is married to Aloo Mistry, the sister of SP Group chairman Shapoor Mistry.Representatives of Tata Sons and Shapoorji Pallonji Group did not offer any immediate comments.SP Group closed one of the largest private credit transactions in India in July, as investors are hopeful that the conglomerate can eventually monetise its stake in Tata Sons and unlock liquidity worth billions of rupees.There’s no certainty that the ongoing talks will lead to a deal and the structure of the transaction may change as negotiations proceed, the sources said. A major hurdle will be in agreeing at a valuation for Tata Sons that controls bulk of the sprawling salt-to-software conglomerate and has many large unlisted businesses such as Air India Ltd and iPhone maker Tata Electronics Pvt Ltd under its umbrella. Both sides are evaluating legal aspects of all options being discussed as well as potential regulatory issues around the share swap since it will involve listed Tata entities, the sources said. SP Group is also periodically updating its stakeholders on the negotiations, while advisers are examining the legal implications of the various structures under consideration, they said.A resolution needs to come through within the next 18 months as that is the timeline when SP Group’s recently closed bond issue will need to make its first payout. These bonds sold by Eqyizen Investment offered 18.95% and will mature in 36 months. The first interest payment is coming up in July 2028.
Article Summary: Tata Group in talks with Shapoorji Pallonji for potential share swap or buyout of its 18.4% stake in Tata Sons. SP Group closed one of the largest private credit transactions in India in July. Investors are hopeful that the conglomerate can eventually monetise its stake.

Article Title: Sensex, Nifty rebound after 2-day losing streak, IT gains
Article Text:
Sensex, Nifty rebound on IT stock rally; Sensex climbs 331 points to 77,265, Nifty gains 85 points to 24,176.

MUMBAI: Benchmark equity indices sensex and Nifty rebounded on Friday after two days of losses and ended higher, tracking buying in blue-chip IT stocks and a rally in global markets. The 30-share BSE sensex climbed 331 points to settle at 77,265. During the day, it jumped 424 points to 77,358 points. The 50-share NSE Nifty, meanwhile, settled 85 points higher at 24,176 points.“Strong gains in IT stocks helped Indian equities close higher today. The sector was supported by Nvidia’s strong earnings and upbeat outlook, which reinforced optimism around sustained AI-related investments. However, investor participation remained selective as markets awaited comments from the Fed Chair at the Jackson Hole symposium for greater clarity on the US interest-rate outlook and global liquidity conditions,” Vinod Nair, head of research, Geojit Investments, said.According to Hariselvan Radhakrishnan, founder & CEO of HST Wealth, a research analyst firm, investors remained positive on IT stocks amid supportive global cues for the sector. “Indian equity benchmarks ended higher on Friday, snapping a two-session losing streak as strong gains in technology stocks offset subdued performance across much of broader market. Technology stocks were session’s clear outperformers, with the Nifty IT index surging 3.5 per cent as investors responded positively to supportive global cues for the sector,” Radhakrishnan said.

Article Title: RBI push: Forex reserves at all-time high of $729.3bn
Article Text:
India Inc sales growth accelerates to 19.4 per cent in Q1 FY27, manufacturing leads recovery: RBI

MUMBAI: The country’s foreign exchange reserves rose by $12.4 billion in the week ended Aug 21, to an all-time high of $729.3 billion, driven largely by non-resident deposits drawn through a special scheme under which RBI took over the foreign currency risks from banks. Foreign currency assets, the largest component, rose $9.5 billion to $591.3 billion, while gold reserves increased $2.8 billion to $114.2 billion.The previous record was $728.5 billion on Feb 27, 2026, just before the outbreak of the US-Iran war. Higher crude oil prices and pressure on the rupee subsequently prompted RBI intervention, taking reserves to a low of $666.9 billion on June 26.The largest weekly increase in total reserves was recorded in the week ended Aug 27, 2021, when reserves rose sharply following a major allocation of special drawing rights by the IMF.For the financial year so far, total reserves have increased by $38.2 billion from end-March 2026. FCA have risen $39.1 billion, more than the overall increase, while gold reserves have declined $1.2 billion.The recent rise in reserves, particularly FCA, has been supported by RBI measures to attract dollar inflows and manage rupee volatility. In June, RBI and govt launched a concessional USD-INR forex swap facility for FCNR(B) deposits, overseas foreign currency borrowings and ECBs.The facility has mobilised an estimated $65 billion to $73 billion ahead of its Aug 31 closure.
Article Summary: Foreign currency assets, the largest component, rose $9.5 billion to $591.3 billion, while gold reserves increased $2.8 billion. The previous record was $728.5billion on Feb 27, 2026, just before the outbreak of the US-Iran war.

Article Title: Industrial output expands 6.7% in July on manufacturing, power
Article Text:
Industrial production grows 6.7% in July, driven by manufacturing and electricity, cooling from June's 8.8%.

NEW DELHI: Industrial production grew 6.7% in July as compared to 5.4% expansion a year ago as the manufacturing and electricity sector saw robust growth, the index of industrial production (IIP) data released Friday showed.Sequentially, the industrial production cooled from an upward revised figure of 8.8% in June. For the first four months of the financial year 2026-27, the IIP growth stood at 6.3%, as compared to 4% in the previous financial year.Among the sub sectors – the manufacturing sector, which has a weight of 76% in the index, grew 7.3%, as 19 out of 23 industry groups witnessed positive growth. This included industries like engineering (electric and non-electrical) and automobiles (all kinds of transport), besides electronics and plastic and rubber products, beverages, wood, paper, and non-metallic minerals. Along with, the capital goods (16.1%), intermediate goods (10%) and infra goods (6.9%) sector also did well, which is a positive sign for the revival in manufacturing, which has been on the cards for some time.“The push given by govt to infra in the four months has forged strong backward linkages,” said Bank of Baroda chief economist Madan Sabnavis. The industries, which lagged in terms of negative growth were, tobacco products, apparel, chemicals, pharma. Export markets were subdued for textiles and pharma, which could have affected growth, in the face of renewed hostilities in West Asia, which threaten to disrupt supply chains.Electricity and gas supply (8.7%) recorded robust expansion on account of heat wave conditions. water supply, sewage and waste management. Newly added industrial activity group, grew 7.4%.
Article Summary: Industrial production grew 6.7% in July as compared to 5.4% expansion a year ago. 19 out of 23 industry groups witnessed positive growth. For the first four months of the financial year 2026-27, the IIP growth stood at 6.3%.

Article Title: Credit, debit cards sharply losing market share to UPI
Article Text:
Payment Bill rekindles MDR hopes for large-value UPI

MUMBAI: India's digital merchant payments market grew 19.6% year-on-year to Rs 11.7 lakh crore in July, but the more consequential change was in how that money moved: UPI's share of person-to-merchant transactions reached a record 77.3%, while credit and debit cards continued to lose ground.According to a report on digital payments by Equirus, UPI's share of M transactions rose 243 basis points year-on-year from 74.9% in July 2025 and increased 22 basis points from June 2026. UPI is increasingly becoming the default payment rail for both retail purchases and merchant transactions, helped by its ubiquity and ease of use.Credit cards, by contrast, are growing more slowly than the market they once benefited from. Their share of merchant payments fell to 17.7% in July 2026 from 19.8% a year earlier, a decline of 203 basis points and below their trailing 12-month average of about 19%.Debit cards fared worse: their share declined to 3.2% from 3.9% reflecting the continued migration of direct bank-account spending to UPI.
Article Summary: India's digital merchant payments market grew 19.6% year-on-year to Rs 11.7 lakh crore in July. UPI's share of person-to-merchant transactions reached a record 77.3%. credit and debit cards continued to lose ground.

Article Title: ‘Unfounded’: Reliance Industries rejects allegations by Subhash Chandra
Article Text:
Reliance Industries has denied allegations made by Essel Group chairman Subhash Chandra. Chandra claimed Ambani's media group conducted a witch hunt against him. He also alleged associates manipulated Zee's share price and used shell entities. Chandra further stated Ambani sought to acquire Zee in collusion with an investor. Lenders are now challenging a tribunal-approved settlement in Chandra's insolvency case.

MUMBAI: Reliance Industries has rejected allegations by Essel Group chairman Subhash Chandra against its media businesses, describing the claims as unfounded, even as some lenders prepare to challenge a tribunal-approved settlement in his insolvency proceedings. A spokesperson for the Mukesh Ambani-controlled conglomerate said the group was “dismayed” by Chandra’s remarks and denied any suggestion that its media platforms had been used to target individuals.“Our media brands have never been used to attack anyone, nor will they ever be,” the spokesperson said, adding that Reliance continued to hold Chandra “in high regard” as a businessman and entrepreneur.The comments come amid a dispute over the resolution of Chandra’s insolvency case, which involves admitted claims of Rs 22,006 crore and has drawn objections from a section of creditors. On his news channel, Chandra alleged a ‘witch hunt’ against him by Ambani’s media group and said it had published false reports that NCLT had cleared Zee’s debt for only Rs 6.5 crore. He also alleged that Ambani’s associates had orchestrated a 40% crash in Zee’s share price in a single day in Jan 2019, when his financial difficulties had begun. He further claimed that Ambani’s associates operated “hundreds and thousands of benami shell entities” to conduct stock market operations, making their involvement difficult to trace.Chandra also alleged that Ambani had later sought to take over Zee in collusion with Invesco, then a Zee investor. He said the proposed transaction would have been financially beneficial to his family but unfair to minority shareholders, prompting Zee shareholders to reject it.
Article Summary: Chandra claimed Ambani's media group conducted a witch hunt against him. Also alleged associates manipulated Zee's share price and used shell entities. Chandra further stated Ambani sought to acquire Zee in collusion with an investor. Lenders are now challenging a tribunal-approved settlement in Chandra's insolvency case.

Article Title: Private companies first quarter sales accelerate but costs drag profit growth
Article Text:
Corporate sales growth accelerated to 19.4% in Q1FY27 but net profit growth slowed to 14.1% as input costs and taxes rose.

Net Profit Grows 14.1% YoY, Slower Than 17.6% In Q1FY26

MUMBAI: The private corporate sector began FY27 with a marked acceleration in sales, but the improvement was less impressive at the bottom line as rising input costs and tax provisions absorbed much of the gain. An analysis of listed non-financial companies by Reserve Bank of India showed sales rising 19.4% year-on-year to Rs 21.6 lakh crore in Q1FY27, up sharply from 5.5% in Q1FY26 and 13.9% in Q4FY26.Net profit, by contrast, grew 14.1% year-on-year to Rs 2.3 lakh crore, slower than the 17.6% growth in Q1FY26 and 27.1% in Q4FY26. Operating profit offered a more encouraging picture, growing 19.3%, compared with 7.3% in Q1FY26 and 9.8% in Q4FY26. The divergence suggests that companies retained considerable operating momentum, but rising costs, following supply-chain disruptions caused by the war in West Asia, and higher tax provisions constrained what reached the bottom line.The main culprit was expenditure. Total expenditure rose 20.8% in Q1FY27, compared with 5.2% in Q1FY26 and 15.1% in Q4FY26. Raw-material costs increased 25.3%, accelerating from 4.8% and 17.8% in the two preceding periods.Power and fuel expenses, meanwhile, rose 19.3%, reversing declines of 6.1% in Q1FY26 and 4.7% in Q4FY26. Tax provisions recorded the sharpest increase among the major expense items, rising 26.3% year-on-year. Interest expenses were the lone major expense category to decline, falling 0.4% year-on-year in Q1FY27.The sectoral picture was broadly supportive. Sales growth among information-technology companies strengthened to 14.8% year-on-year in Q1FY27 from 9.9% in the previous quarter. Non-IT services companies continued to record double-digit growth of 19.7%, only marginally below 20.3% in the previous quarter, led mainly by wholesale and retail trade.Labour costs also gathered steady pace. Staff costs at manufacturing, IT and non-IT services companies rose 12.4%, 7.6% and 11.2%, respectively, in Q1FY27, higher than their growth in the previous quarter. Staff cost as a share of sales increased to 5.5% for manufacturing companies and 10.1% for non-IT services companies. For IT companies, however, the ratio declined from the previous quarter.There was also evidence that companies retained some pricing power despite the squeeze on inputs. Operating-profit growth at manufacturing companies accelerated sharply to 21.3% year-on-year in Q1FY27 from 9.4% in the previous quarter. IT and non-IT services companies also saw operating-profit growth improve to 19.9% and 12.7%, respectively, during Q1FY27.
Article Summary: Net profit grew 14.1% year-on-year to Rs 2.3 lakh crore, slower than 17.6% growth in Q1FY26. Rising input costs and tax provisions absorbed much of the gain. Raw-material costs increased 25.3%, accelerating from 4.8% and 17.8%. Power and fuel expenses, meanwhile, rose 19.3%.

Article Title: Buffalo dairies increase milk price by record Rs 9 per litre in Mumbai
Article Text:
(Representative image) The Bombay Milk Producers Association has decided to raise the wholesale prices of buffalo milk, effective from September 1st

MUMBAI: The Bombay Milk Producers' Association has raised the wholesale rate of buffalo milk by a record nine rupees from Rs 93 to Rs 102 per litre.The new rates will take effect Sept 1 and will come up for review on Feb 28, 2027.Retail prices will rise correspondingly higher.Association president CK Singh said, "The increase was necessitated by the spiralling cost of animal feed, fodder and sundry items required for milk production. From milch animals to grain, tuvar and chana feed to corn, we are witnessing a hike of upto 25%. Grass and fodder is also far costlier. It is not viable to continue to sell milk at the old rate."The members of the dairy association unanimously agreed on this increase which is the largest in recent history.
Article Summary: Bombay Milk Producers' Association has raised the wholesale rate of buffalo milk by a record nine rupees. The new rates will take effect Sept 1 and will come up for review on Feb 28, 2027. The increase was necessitated by the spiralling cost of animal feed, fodder and sundry items required for milk production.

Article Title: RRB NTPC UG CBT 2 exam on September 17, check city slip and admit card dates
Article Text:
RRB NTPC UG CBT 2 2026 exam date announced, check key dates, pattern and selection process

RRB NTPC UG CBT 2

exam 2026:

RRB NTPC UG CBT 2 key dates

Event Date City Intimation Slip and SC/ST Travel Pass September 7, 2026 CBT 2 Admit Card September 13, 2026 CBT 2 Examination September 17, 2026 Tentative Typing Skill Test/CBAT December 4, 2026

45,898 candidates shortlisted for CBT 2

The Railway Recruitment Boards (RRBs) have announced the date for the RRB NTPC Undergraduate (UG) CBT 2 examination under CEN 07/2025. The second-stage computer-based test is scheduled for September 17, 2026, following the declaration of the CBT 1 results and scorecards.The official notice confirming the CBT 2 schedule was released on August 24, 2026. Article Title: Inflation isn’t meaningfully slowing: Federal Reserve chairman
Article Text:
Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh speaks on inflation

Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh warned inflation isn’t meaningfully slowing and said policymakers must be confident that it is, otherwise the central bank has “work to do. ” In a sweeping speech, his first since becoming chairman of the central bank in May, Warsh reiterated that policymakers will return inflation to their 2% goal, which he said is a firm and fixed target.“Here is my standard: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do. That’s our job,” Warsh said in remarks prepared for Fed’s annual conference in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.Warsh said financial conditions are not restrictive and interest rates are Fed’s “predominant tool” for achieving its mandate, though he stopped short of signaling he would support an interest-rate hike when Fed officials gather in Sept. “I stand here today committed to a discipline, not to a decision.” Yields for two-year Treasuries rose five basis points to 4.28%, while 30-year rates slipped — signal of an expectation that Fed may need to raise short-term rates.
Article Summary: Warsh reiterated that policymakers will return inflation to their 2% goal. Yields for two-year Treasuries rose five basis points to 4.28%. 30-year rates slipped — signal of an expectation that Fed may need to raise short-term rates.

Article Title: Oil prices today: Crude holds steady, heads for weekly losses as Hormuz flows remain choppy
Article Text:
Goldman Sachs estimated that total Gulf exports recently stood at 15 million to 16 million barrels per day (representative image)

Hormuz traffic remains uneven

MCX crude slips nearly 1%

Oil prices were largely steady on Friday but remained on track for a sharp weekly decline as traders weighed stalled US-Iran diplomatic talks against a tentative and uneven recovery in crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz.Brent crude futures were down 4 cents at $89.66 a barrel at 0943 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude fell 32 cents, or 0.38%, to $83.21 a barrel.Both benchmarks were set to end the week lower, with Brent down 5.1% and WTI declining 4.5%.“A combination of US tactics moving to economic sanctions rather than military pressure and talks of Oman-Iran's joint corridor have led to risk premiums declining,” Suvro Sarkar, head of energy research at DBS Bank, told Reuters.The US announced what it called the “toughest sanctions in history” on Iran earlier this week. Tehran described the sanctions as an “inhumane and hostile act” that had lost their effectiveness.The Strait of Hormuz, through which around 20% of the world's oil supply moves, has seen a tentative recovery in shipping, although flows remain uneven.Preliminary shipping data showed that seven commodity vessels transited the waterway on Thursday, down from 17 a day earlier and below the 10-day average of 15, Reuters reported.At the Bab el-Mandeb, another major maritime chokepoint, 17 commodity vessels passed through, with six entering and 11 exiting.Goldman Sachs estimated that total Gulf exports recently stood at 15 million to 16 million barrels per day, around 7 million to 8 million bpd below pre-war levels but 5 million to 6 million bpd above the lowest point recorded in March.“We are of the attitude of being prepared for everything but predicting nothing,” PVM Oil Futures analyst John Evans said, adding that several factors, including OPEC developments and China's demand, remained linked to the wider conflict.In India, crude oil futures also traded lower on Friday. Crude futures for September delivery on the Multi Commodity Exchange (MCX) fell Rs 49, or nearly 1%, to Rs 7,915 per barrel.The October contract declined Rs 56, or 0.71%, to Rs 7,797 per barrel.Analysts cited by news agency PTI said that reports of a possible US role in Venezuela's oil industry weighed on prices as traders assessed the possibility of increased output from the South American producer.Anindya Banerjee, head of commodity and currency research at Kotak Securities, said Brent was trading lower as Washington's shift from military to economic pressure had reduced fears of a wider war.He added that Iran and Oman had reached a partial arrangement on sharing revenue from Hormuz traffic, although Tehran has said a full deal remains blocked.“The easing in prices reflects a market moving away from extreme conditions, although the underlying supply remains tight,” Banerjee said.
Article Summary: Brent crude futures were down 4 cents at $89.66 a barrel at 0943 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude fell 32 cents, or 0.38%, to $83.21 a barrel. Both benchmarks were set to end the week lower, with Brent down 5.1% and WTI declining 4.5%.

Article Title: US debt crosses $40 trillion: But who does Uncle Sam owe money to?
Article Text:
Trump is adding to a US debt pile that has been building for decades under both parties.

What is national debt, anyway?

At around 124% of US GDP, the $40tn debt pile is larger than the entire annual economic output of the country.

So who does Uncle Sam actually owe?

At around 124% of US GDP, the $40tn debt pile is larger than the entire annual economic output of the country.

Trump's debt bill so far

Trump’s second-term debt accumulation is already moving faster than during his first term

The bond market's verdict

The pace of borrowing has changed dramatically: the latest $1tn was added in less than five months, compared with 205 years for the first.

The bill keeps coming

Forty trillion dollars. Written out in full, that is $40,000,000,000,000, a four followed by thirteen zeros.Spend a dollar every second, and it would take more than 1.2 million years to get through the whole amount. Or stack that same sum in $100 bills, one on top of the other, and the pile would reach around 27,000 miles into the sky, enough to wrap right around the Earth with room to spare.On August 18, the US Treasury confirmed that America's national debt had crossed exactly that mark for the first time in history, months earlier than most forecasters expected just a year ago. That works out to roughly $117,000 for every American, or nearly $297,000 per household.Numbers this size stop meaning much after a while. But they raise one genuinely interesting question. Who does the world's biggest economy owe to?Every year a government spends more than it collects in tax, the shortfall is called a deficit. Governments cover that gap by borrowing, mostly by selling Treasury bonds, bills and notes to investors. Add up enough years of deficits and you end up with a national debt.Think of it like a mortgage or a business loan. Borrowing money is not automatically reckless.What matters is what the money is spent on, and whether the economy grows quickly enough to make the borrowing worthwhile.Countries have used debt for centuries to fund wars, recover from crises, and build the infrastructure and technology that drive future growth. If the economy grows faster than the cost of borrowing, the debt becomes easier to carry over time. That is roughly what happened after the Second World War. Debt held by the public reached around 106% of GDP, then decades of strong postwar growth steadily brought the ratio down, without America ever needing to pay off the whole debt in one go.Japan shows just how much debt an advanced economy can carry without collapsing. Its debt-to-GDP ratio sits above 200%, the highest of any major economy, and has done for years. Most of that debt is held domestically and in yen, which shields Japan from the kind of panic that hits countries reliant on foreign lenders.America has a similar cushion. The dollar is the world's dominant reserve currency, and US Treasuries are seen as one of the world's safest assets, which keeps investors willing to lend Washington money.The real concern is not that America has debt. It is the maths behind it. Interest rates have climbed sharply since 2022, and the cost of servicing the debt is now rising faster than the economy itself, a very different picture to the cheap-borrowing years of the 2010s.This is where the $40tn figure gets interesting.Start with the $7.78tn in intragovernmental debt, roughly a fifth of the total. Think of it as the government moving money from one of its own pockets to another. The largest holder is the Social Security Trust Fund, which holds around $2.3tn. When payroll taxes bring in more than the programme pays out in benefits, the surplus is invested in special Treasury securities, essentially one arm of government holding an IOU from another.The remaining $32.27tn is debt held by the public, and this is where the "who does America owe" question really begins.The biggest slice belongs to domestic private investors. American mutual funds, banks, insurers, pension funds and households collectively hold around $17.9tn, or roughly 57% of publicly held debt. If you have a pension or an index fund with any bond exposure, there is a decent chance you are quietly one of Uncle Sam's creditors yourself.The Federal Reserve holds a further $4.4-4.5tn through its own bond portfolio, close to 14%.Foreign investors hold around $9.35tn, roughly 29% of publicly held debt, and less than a quarter of the full $40tn once intragovernmental debt is included.Here the popular image usually gets it wrong. China is not the biggest foreign holder, and has not been for years. That title belongs to Japan, a close US ally, which holds around $1.21tn. The UK comes second at roughly $937bn. China sits third at around $651bn, having steadily cut its exposure from a 2013 peak of $1.32tn as Beijing diversifies its reserves. Further down the list sit Belgium, the Cayman Islands, Luxembourg and Ireland, all financial centres, so their large holdings often belong to investors based elsewhere entirely, simply routed through custodians there.The US Treasury does not owe these countries one giant loan. It owes millions of investors through a constantly rolling market of Treasury securities. Even Japan's $1.21tn holding is nowhere near enough to dictate America's borrowing costs on its own.Add it up and roughly four-fifths of America's $40tn is owed to Americans, American institutions or the government itself.The popular image of America being indebted to the rest of the world is therefore misleading. Uncle Sam’s debt is overwhelmingly homegrown.Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, the debt has grown by around $3.8tn in about nineteen months. Combined with the $7.8tn added in his first term, his two terms have so far added roughly $11.6tn. For comparison, the debt grew by about $8.4tn across Joe Biden's four years, from roughly $27.8tn to $36.2tn, so the current pace is running noticeably faster.A large chunk of the recent rise came from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the tax and spending package Trump signed into law in July 2025, which the Congressional Budget Office estimates will add around $4tn to the deficit over the next decade, largely through extended tax cuts. Rising defence spending, including the cost of this year's war with Iran, has added further pressure, alongside the lost tariff revenue outlined earlier.But the debt problem does not belong to one president. The US has run persistent deficits under both parties for decades, through tax cuts, wars, recessions and emergency spending. The $40tn figure is simply the accumulated bill.The $40tn figure tells us how much America owes. The bond market helps determine how much it costs to keep owing it.Think of the US government as someone with a giant mortgage that never quite gets paid off. Every time part of that mortgage comes due, it borrows again to pay it off. As long as lenders are happy to keep offering roughly the same interest rate, the arrangement can continue without too much trouble.The problem starts when those lenders ask for more.That is essentially what Treasury yields tell us. A Treasury yield is the interest rate investors demand to lend money to the US government. When yields rise, Washington has to pay more to borrow. And because the US has to keep refinancing huge amounts of existing debt while borrowing more to cover its deficit, even a small increase in rates can eventually add billions to the government's interest bill.That is why the bond market matters to the $40tn story.On the day the debt crossed $40tn, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced plans to at least double some long-term Treasury buyback operations, from $2bn to at least $4bn per operation. The move came as a bond sell-off pushed the 30-year Treasury yield as high as 5.34%, its highest level since 2007.The announcement briefly pushed yields lower before they drifted back up within a day. That is because a buyback can help manage the supply of bonds in the market, but it does not fix the underlying deficit. It is more like rearranging the mortgage than reducing the amount you owe.The reason investors are jumpy is in the numbers. The federal deficit is running at around 5.8% of GDP, well above the 3.8% average of the past 50 years. Interest costs alone eat up about 3.3% of GDP and are now one of the fastest-growing items in the federal budget.The risk is a feedback loop. If borrowing costs stay above the pace at which the economy grows, the debt becomes harder to stabilise. Rising interest costs can then require more borrowing, putting further pressure on rates.America's first trillion dollars of debt took 205 years to accumulate, arriving in October 1981. The most recent trillion, the climb from $39tn to $40tn, took under five months. Ten trillion came in 2008, twenty trillion in 2017, thirty trillion in 2022, and now forty trillion in 2026, each milestone arriving faster than the last.None of that means the sky is falling. America can still borrow in its own currency, and investors around the world still buy its debt when markets turn nervous. What has changed is the price of that comfort.The $40tn figure is not a crisis on its own. It is the accumulated bill for decades of tax cuts, wars, recessions and political promises made by presidents and Congresses of both parties.The US can keep rolling the debt over. But the interest bill keeps coming due.
Article Summary: The $40tn debt pile is larger than the entire annual economic output of the country. It would take more than 1.2 million years to get through the whole amount. The largest holder is the Social Security Trust Fund, which holds around $2.3tn.

Article Title: 'Time to teach Canada': Trump rails as trade war gets ugly
Article Text:
Trump warns Canada amid tariff dispute

US president Donald Trump has warned Canada of possible further action, saying it was “time to teach Canada you can't do this anymore,” as trade tensions between the two countries intensify.Canada on Tuesday announced retaliatory tariffs of up to 50% on more than 700 US products worth around $27.6 billion, escalating its trade dispute with the United States.Canadian prime minister Mark Carney accused Washington of seeking to subordinate Canada, saying US demands during the failed trade negotiations showed that Americans wanted to “destroy our major industries”, including autos, steel and aluminium.The new tariffs, set to take effect on September 8, will cover a broad range of American goods, including fish, cheese, honey, cosmetics, clothing, household appliances, smartphones, motorcycles, and steel and aluminium products.The tariffs will be imposed at rates of 15%, 25% and 50%, with the highest rate applying to several products, including certain dairy, cosmetics and lumber items. Canada will also increase tariffs on US steel and aluminium products from 25% to 50%, CBC News reported.Ottawa said the measures target products “most affected by US tariffs” and are intended to match the duties imposed by Washington in its latest round of tariffs.Canada’s latest measures extend beyond industrial goods, targeting everyday products such as cheese, toilet paper, clothing, smartphones and household appliances.Trade tensions have continued to escalate, with Trump threatening further tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel.He said his administration would raise tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts and steel to 50% from January 1, 2027.Carney said the proposed auto tariffs would “gradually dismantle” Canada’s vehicle production industry.Trump also added another point of friction on Tuesday, saying the US was giving “serious consideration” to renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America”, amid his ongoing dispute with Ontario Premier Doug Ford.
Article Summary: Canada announces retaliatory tariffs of up to 50% on more than 700 US products worth around $27.6 billion. New tariffs, set to take effect on September 8, will cover a broad range of American goods. Canada will also increase tariffs on US steel and aluminium products from 25% to 50%.

Article Title: Lord’s Mark Industries Limited and ARKALL Holding Limited partner for healthcare expansion across Caribbean countries
Article Text:
“The Caribbean presents an important opportunity to strengthen healthcare infrastructure through greater access to quality diagnostics, medical technology and specialised healthcare solutions. Our partnership with Lord’s Mark Industries Limited brings together local market capabilities with an expanding portfolio of healthcare technologies.

Beginning with Trinidad & Tobago, our objective is to build a scalable network that can progressively serve healthcare needs across all 28 Caribbean markets.

”

,

”

Lord’s Mark Industries Limited has partnered with Caribbean-based ARKALL Holdings Limited to establish and operate pathology laboratories and expand the commercialisation of its medical devices, equipment and healthcare portfolio across 28 Caribbean marketsThis marks Lord’s Mark Industries Limited’s first entry into the Caribbean market and one of the largest-scale entries by an Indian healthcare company into the region, with a broad portfolio of pre-approved products spanning diagnostics, MedTech and healthcare solutions.The partnership will commence with Trinidad & Tobago and progressively expand across the wider Caribbean over the next three years, according to the company. Article Summary: Lord’s Mark Industries Limited has partnered with Caribbean-based ARKALL Holdings Limited to establish and operate pathology laboratories.
